item.title: 29 Fake Bank Sites Caught Using the Same Contact Details to Steal Logins
item.description:
A bank doesn’t necessarily need a real branch, banking licence, or even a genuine business to look convincing online anymore. A phishing campaign Netskope Threat Labs discovered reveals that cybercriminals can create fictional but genuine-looking banks, with account-opening pages, customer support details, and online banking portals, using just a ready-made PHP script.

Researchers report that around 29 fake-bank domains appeared over seven weeks- starting in late September 2026- using names like Sunray Trust, Quartz Bank, Western Future Bank and Apex Trust Financial Bank. These pages were designed to collect login credentials and personally identifiable information (PII), including names and addresses.

Geographically, North America had the most affected organizations, followed by Europe and Asia whereas Finance and banking organizations had nearly half of the victims.

Same Bank, Different Names

Fake banking sites may look like separate financial institutions to an unsuspecting visitor, but Netskope found that they share the same underlying template. Their layouts, marketing text, support number (1-800-BANKING) and even bank routing number (251480576) are identical, apart from one deployment that changes a digit to 981480576.

The sites appeared to belong to different banks, but Netskope Threat Labs traced them to a single phishing kit. The kit gave scammers a ready-made banking website with login and account-opening forms designed to collect passwords and personal information. They could change the bank name and reuse the rest. On six sites Netskope examined, the same layout, tagline and support number showed up again, along with a routing number that differed by one digit on one site.

One detail left behind on the now offline Quartz Bank’s website (qtbnk.com) offered a clue about where the pages came from. Its logo carried the original template branding: “EMENDY INVEST, Bitcoin, forex investment and trading PHP script.”

Researchers believe that the operators acquired or traded a ready-made PHP banking script and reused it with different bank names, and also used low-cost or abuse-friendly domain extensions, including .sbs, .cc, .pro, .live, .online and .info. The site Sunray Trust (sunraytrustbn.sbs) was detected just a day after its domain was registered.

Scammers have tried their best to make these fictional banks look established. Netskope found Bray Finance listed as the contact on a real estate website while another fake bank appeared on a business information site linking directly to its phishing domain. Such listings could help these names appear in search engines and AI-generated answers, Netskope notes, which will give victims another reason to trust them.

Why Domain Reputation Is Not Enough

Around one-third of the 29 domains had no VirusTotal detections when Netskope first found them, while the remaining domains averaged fewer than five detections across approximately 90 antivirus and URL-scanning engines. Researchers also spotted an Allyunity Bank version with a CAPTCHA-evasion variant.

“These sites live fast and die young,” Netskope researchers wrote in the blog post shared with Hackread.com, explaining that operators can abandon domains before reputation-based security tools have time to flag them.

List of sites spotted in the scam:

qtbnk.com
norexgo.com
1stggbinc.cc
oakmontfb.com
allyunitybn.com
gulfcoastcu.org
premiummaya.com
vaultroyalb.com
ardenovabank.com
glariontrust.com
kinoxcapital.com
northgatebnk.com
bank.firstcp.live
sunraytrustbn.sbs
brayfinance.online
corepayfinance.com
heritageprivate.cc
sterlingtrusts.pro
alliancetrustcu.pro
apextrustfinbank.com
westernfuturebnk.com
westlinedigital.info
clyntelitecapital.com
northfieldreserve.com
swiftpremiumcapital.com
hyperionglobalholdings.com
globalheritagestandards.com
securecapitalcorporationlimited.com
ubnazionale.live.loadingloading.com.ng

Hackread.com has previously covered ready-made banking phishing tools, including the Spiderman kit, which cloned legitimate European banks and cryptocurrency services; however, this campaign takes a different approach altogether. It doesn’t impersonate established banks; it gives criminals fictional financial institutions they can put online using the same template.

The important clue for defenders is that the domain name may change, but the website’s underlying details do not. Repeated routing numbers, contact information and page elements can expose the next fake bank even before security scanners recognise its domain.

item.title: F5 Patches Two NGINX HTTP/2 Vulnerabilities, One Dating Back to (2015)
item.description:
F5 has released security updates for two critical vulnerabilities in NGINX, the open-source web server owned and maintained by F5, powering more than 225 million websites.

These vulnerabilities can allow attackers to execute code on affected servers without authentication, exposing websites, APIs and the applications running behind them. The flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633 with a CVSS score of 9.2.

What’s interesting is that they were independently investigated and reported to F5 by five research teams, including Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7 and Xint. Per their findings, both flaws are in NGINX’s HTTP/2 implementation and not in the websites or applications using the software.

Wiz’s research, shared with Hackread.com, provides a detailed overview of the security impact of the issue. Wiz researchers used the AI-powered Wiz Atlas platform to identify the flaws and Gemini 4 Carbon and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to validate their findings.

They successfully carried out remote code execution (RCE) on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds. This included a server delivering ordinary static files without a backend application or third-party modules. Both vulnerabilities, however, require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected server.

The NGINX disclosures come just a day after the discovery of Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)- a critical OpenJDK vulnerability reported by Calif that can also lead to unauthenticated remote code execution.


The Vulnerabilities


CVE-2026-123007 is an integer underflow in HTTP/2 flow-control accounting. It affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5, released in 2015. Incorrect handling of unused data allowances can eventually cause an out-of-bounds memory operation.

The other flaw, CVE-2026-123633, is a use-after-free vulnerability affecting versions 1.19.7 to 1.31.8. It can occur during reverse-proxy processing when NGINX runs low on available connection slots.


NGINX is a recurring target


This isn’t the first time NGINX has faced attacks involving AI-assisted vulnerability research. In May, Hackread.com reported attacks exploiting NGINX Rift (CVE-2026-42945). That flaw was different, though, because it required a specific, non-default rewrite configuration and mainly exposed servers to denial-of-service (DoS) attacks, whereas RCE was possible only when ASLR was disabled or bypassed.

The latest vulnerabilities are far riskier because they let unauthenticated attackers execute code on affected servers. A successful attack can give them control over systems handling traffic for multiple websites and applications and this would put customer data and services at risk.

Patches and Updates


In its November 18 security update, F5 addressed ten NGINX vulnerabilities, including additional flaws affecting HTTP/3, the DNS resolver and mail proxy modules, and issues that could cause DoS or other security problems. The fixes address both critical HTTP/2 flaws.

Administrators should update NGINX Open Source to 1.30.7 (stable) or 1.31.9 (mainline). NGINX Plus users should install the applicable fixed version: 37.0.7.1, 37.0.8.1, 37.2.0.1, or 37.3.0.1.

Those unable to upgrade immediately should temporarily disable HTTP/2 using http2 off in affected server blocks.
For defenders, the key takeaway is that finding vulnerabilities is only half the job; now, they also need to identify affected systems and get the fixes installed before attackers can exploit them.

item.title: Criminal IP Launches AITEM to Connect Asset Discovery with AI-Powered Exposure Management
item.description:
Torrance, California, USA, November 19th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Criminal IP, a cyber threat intelligence platform developed by AI SPERA, officially launched Criminal IP AITEM (AI-Powered Threat Exposure Management) on November 18, 2026. An evolution of Criminal IP ASM, AITEM combines internet-facing asset discovery with AI-assisted investigation, public-source exposure analysis, and dark web monitoring. It also introduces AI Pentest to help security teams assess and validate security risks in their web assets.

Discovering an unfamiliar server or a leaked credential is the first step. Analysts still need to establish how it relates to their organization, assess the surrounding threat signals, and decide whether it requires immediate attention. Criminal IP AITEM brings these findings and their context together so teams can understand what is exposed and decide where to act.

A Broader View of Organizational Exposure

Forgotten servers, publicly accessible configuration files, and compromised credentials can be difficult to assess when findings are scattered across separate tools. Criminal IP AITEM brings these exposures into a single view so teams can investigate them in the context of their environment.

Criminal IP AITEM dashboard summarizes asset inventory, risk distribution, recent findings, and exposure trends

The dashboard gives teams an overview of discovered assets and detected risks. Analysts can drill down into individual assets to investigate specific findings and explore related infrastructure.

Criminal IP AITEM continuously discovers internet-facing assets and collects information such as IP addresses, domains, certificates, open ports, cloud assets, and technologies. Analysts can use these details to understand how an unfamiliar system connects to their organization.

Exposure Beyond Managed Infrastructure

Criminal IP AITEM identifies publicly accessible information through search engine analysis and GitHub exposure detection

Public-source exposure analysis helps teams find sensitive files, administrative pages, and exposed directories indexed by search engines. GitHub exposure detection helps uncover publicly accessible credentials, API keys, and configuration files associated with the organization.

Dark web monitoring surfaces leaked credentials, exposed information, and mentions of the organization across monitored sources. Available source details help analysts assess each finding and decide what to investigate next.

AI Across the Exposure Lifecycle

AI-Powered at Every Step: Detect, Investigate, Prioritize, and Automate

Criminal IP AITEM applies AI across detection, investigation, prioritization, and automation. It connects emerging vulnerabilities with potentially affected assets and supports natural-language queries across assets, vulnerabilities, and exposures, reducing the need for complex filters and repeated manual searches.

Prioritization considers exposure severity, asset impact, and threat context to help teams decide which findings need attention first. Automated alerts and investigation workflows support follow-up and reduce manual tracking as risks change.

For example, when Criminal IP AITEM discovers an unfamiliar server, analysts can review its open ports, exposed services, SSL/TLS configurations, and related CVEs. Criminal IP threat intelligence adds context through connected infrastructure, malicious activity, abuse history, and associated threat indicators. Together, these details help analysts assess the server’s potential impact and decide what to investigate first.

Validating Web Asset Risks with AI Pentest

Criminal IP AITEM’s AI Pentest capability enables security teams to run AI-powered penetration tests on their web assets. Teams can use it to identify potential vulnerabilities and validate suspected security weaknesses, giving them additional evidence to decide which findings require remediation.

Continuous Monitoring as Exposure Changes

As organizations deploy services and work with external suppliers, their exposure changes. Criminal IP AITEM uses daily scans, historical tracking, and automated notifications to help teams follow those changes. Monitoring can also extend to partners and suppliers.

With Criminal IP AITEM, Criminal IP connects asset visibility with exposure investigation and ongoing monitoring. Security teams can better understand what is exposed, why a finding matters, and where to focus their next action.

Learn more about Criminal IP AITEM.

About Criminal IP

Criminal IP is AI SPERA’s flagship cyber threat intelligence platform. Used in more than 150 countries, it provides comprehensive threat visibility through Criminal IP Search, Criminal IP ASM, Criminal IP FDS, and Criminal IP TI Feed.

Criminal IP continues to expand its global security ecosystem through integrations and strategic partnerships. Its threat intelligence is also accessible through major cloud and data marketplaces, including Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Snowflake.

Contact

Michael Sena
AI SPERA

item.title: How to Swap Bitcoin to Ethereum on a Decentralized Exchange
item.description:
To swap Bitcoin to Ethereum on a decentralized exchange (DEX), you need a cross-chain DEX that holds liquidity on both the Bitcoin and Ethereum networks. Most DEXs, such as those built on Ethereum, cannot accept native BTC at all; they only trade wrapped versions of it. THORChain is a decentralized cross-chain exchange that swaps native BTC for native ETH directly from your own wallet, with no account, no deposit to a company and no wrapped token involved.

Why can’t you swap Bitcoin on most DEXs?

A typical DEX lives on a single blockchain. Uniswap, for example, runs on Ethereum and other EVM networks and can only trade tokens that exist on those networks. Bitcoin is a separate blockchain, so native BTC never touches an Ethereum DEX.

What those DEXs trade instead are wrapped versions of Bitcoin, such as WBTC or cbBTC: Ethereum tokens backed by BTC held by a custodian. If you already hold wrapped BTC, you can swap it for ETH on an Ethereum DEX. But if you hold real BTC in a Bitcoin wallet, you first need to convert it into a wrapped token through a custodian or bridge, which adds a step and a party you have to trust.

A cross-chain DEX removes that problem. It holds liquidity on each connected blockchain, takes in BTC on the Bitcoin network and pays out ETH on the Ethereum network.

Centralized exchange vs decentralized exchange for BTC to ETH

A centralized exchange can make sense for frequent traders who want order books and fiat access. A cross-chain DEX suits people who want to keep control of their coins and simply convert BTC into ETH.

How does a cross-chain DEX swap BTC for ETH?

On THORChain, every supported asset sits in a liquidity pool paired with RUNE, the network’s settlement asset. A BTC to ETH swap moves through two pools, BTC to RUNE and then RUNE to ETH, in a single transaction from the user’s point of view. You never need to hold RUNE yourself.

The exchange’s vaults on Bitcoin and Ethereum are controlled jointly by its validators, called THORNodes, using threshold signatures, so no single operator holds the keys. Each node bonds RUNE as collateral that can be slashed for malicious behavior. Swaps within each block are also ordered by price impact, which is designed to resist sandwich attacks and other front-running.

How to swap BTC to ETH on THORChain: the short version

  1. Open a THORChain interface. Use the official THORChain Swap site or a wallet that integrates it. Type the address yourself or use a bookmark to avoid phishing copies.
  2. Choose BTC to ETH and enter the amount. Paste an Ethereum address you control as the destination. It can be a brand-new address, since the Ethereum fee is taken from the output.
  3. Review the quote. Check the expected ETH amount after all fees and the estimated time. For larger trades, turn on streaming swaps if available.
  4. Send the BTC. Sign the transaction in your Bitcoin wallet, or use the walletless option and send BTC to the generated deposit address. Native ETH arrives once the Bitcoin deposit is confirmed and the swap is processed.

What does it cost?

A BTC to ETH swap on a cross-chain DEX has three main costs: the Bitcoin network fee to send your BTC, a liquidity fee that depends on trade size relative to pool depth, and an outbound fee that covers the Ethereum transaction delivering your ETH. Some interfaces add their own fee on top. All of these are shown in the quote, so the number to compare is the ETH you will actually receive.

Small and medium trades generally see low price impact. For large amounts, streaming swaps split the order into smaller pieces executed over time, which reduces price impact in exchange for a longer wait.

How long does it take?

Timing depends mostly on Bitcoin. The exchange waits for enough Bitcoin confirmations before processing the swap, and larger deposits can require more confirmations. After that, the swap and the outbound ETH transaction are usually processed quickly. Interfaces show an estimated time with each quote and a tracker for each stage.

What are the risks?

Using a DEX removes the risk of an exchange freezing or losing your account balance, but it does not remove every risk. While a swap is being processed, your funds pass through the exchange’s vaults, so you rely on its code and validator set during that window. Trading can also be paused during upgrades or incidents, which can delay a swap or trigger a refund. If a swap cannot complete, for example because the price moved beyond your slippage limit, the BTC is refunded to your sending address minus network fees.

The most common user errors are avoidable: pasting a wrong or non-Ethereum destination address, reusing an expired quote, and using a fake interface. If you are new to the process, start with a small test swap.

Frequently asked questions

Can I swap Bitcoin to Ethereum on Uniswap?

Not native bitcoin. Uniswap runs on Ethereum and other EVM networks, so it can only trade wrapped BTC tokens such as WBTC or cbBTC. To swap native BTC for ETH on a decentralized exchange, you need a cross-chain DEX such as THORChain.

Is THORChain a decentralized exchange?

Yes. THORChain is a decentralized cross-chain exchange that swaps native assets between blockchains, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, XRP, Dogecoin and Litecoin, without wrapped tokens.

Do I need an account or KYC to swap BTC to ETH on a DEX?

No account is needed on THORChain. You swap directly from a wallet you control. Some third-party interfaces may apply their own policies, so check the terms of the one you use.

Do I need ETH to receive ETH?

No. The Ethereum network fee for delivering your ETH is deducted from the swap output, so you can receive ETH into an empty Ethereum address.

Is a DEX cheaper than a centralized exchange for BTC to ETH?

It depends on the trade size and the exchange. A DEX avoids deposit and withdrawal steps, while a centralized exchange charges trading and withdrawal fees instead of liquidity fees. Compare the final amount of ETH you would receive on each.

How to swap BTC to ETH on THORChain: the short version

  1. Open a THORChain interface. Use the official THORChain Swap site or a wallet that integrates it. Type the address yourself or use a bookmark to avoid phishing copies.
  2. Choose BTC to ETH and enter the amount. Paste an Ethereum address you control as the destination. It can be a brand-new address, since the Ethereum fee is taken from the output.
  3. Review the quote. Check the expected ETH amount after all fees and the estimated time. For larger trades, turn on streaming swaps if available.

What does it cost?

A BTC to ETH swap on a cross-chain DEX has three main costs: the Bitcoin network fee to send your BTC, a liquidity fee that depends on trade size relative to pool depth, and an outbound fee that covers the Ethereum transaction delivering your ETH. Small and medium trades generally see low price impact. For large amounts, streaming swaps split the order into smaller pieces executed over time, which reduces price impact in exchange for a longer wait.

Timing depends mostly on Bitcoin. The exchange waits for enough Bitcoin confirmations before processing the swap, and larger deposits can require more confirmations. What are the risks?

Using a DEX removes the risk of an exchange freezing or losing your account balance, but it does not remove every risk. The most common user errors are avoidable: pasting a wrong or non-Ethereum destination address, reusing an expired quote, and using a fake interface. If you are new to the process, start with a small test swap.

Frequently asked questions

Can I swap Bitcoin to Ethereum on Uniswap?

Not native bitcoin. Uniswap runs on Ethereum and other EVM networks, so it can only trade wrapped BTC tokens such as WBTC or cbBTC. To swap native BTC for ETH on a decentralized exchange, you need a cross-chain DEX such as THORChain.

Yes. THORChain is a decentralized cross-chain exchange that swaps native assets between blockchains, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, XRP, Dogecoin and Litecoin, without wrapped tokens.

No account is needed on THORChain. You swap directly from a wallet you control. Some third-party interfaces may apply their own policies, so check the terms of the one you use.

Do I need ETH to receive ETH?

No. The Ethereum network fee for delivering your ETH is deducted from the swap output, so you can receive ETH into an empty Ethereum address.

It depends on the trade size and the exchange. A DEX avoids deposit and withdrawal steps, while a centralized exchange charges trading and withdrawal fees instead of liquidity fees. Compare the final amount of ETH you would receive on each.

item.title: Comparing Crypto Payment Processors for International Merchants
item.description:
International merchants already manage several payment variables at once: what customers can use, which currencies suppliers expect, and when funds reach the operating business. Accepting cryptocurrency adds another layer to that work. The processor needs to connect digital asset payments with accounting, conversion, settlement, and, in some cases, outbound transfers.

Start with the settlement currency

A crypto payment gateway can collect Bitcoin, Ethereum, stablecoins, and other supported assets through invoices, hosted payment pages, payment links, plugins, or a direct API connection. The point at which the merchant receives spendable funds is a separate decision.

Fiat settlement converts received assets into conventional money, such as USD, EUR, or GBP. Stablecoin settlement delivers assets such as USDT or USDC, which are designed to maintain a reference value. A business might also retain certain cryptocurrencies. Each method changes the treasury workflow, liquidity planning, and exposure to price movements.

Stablecoins became particularly relevant to cross-border commerce because blockchain transfers can offer quicker movement of funds than some banking routes. Their relatively stable denomination can make invoice amounts and outgoing transfers easier to plan. Merchants must still consider network selection, custody arrangements, redemption exposure, and access to the required jurisdictions.

What belongs in a processor review

A merchant should examine more than the number of supported coins. The following checks directly affect payment operations:

  • Coverage in the countries where customers and counterparties operate
  • Support for required coins, stablecoins, and blockchain networks
  • Time needed to make received funds available for use
  • Fiat conversion, stablecoin settlement, and currency preferences
  • KYB, AML screening, applicable licenses, and settlement records
  • API documentation, plugins, invoices, and reconciliation data
  • Availability of batch or individual business payouts

Geographic coverage needs special attention because services offered under one brand may differ by contracting entity. A supported coin doesn’t guarantee a matching fiat account, conversion route, or payout destination. Request the settlement terms for each entity and currency, including when a converted balance becomes withdrawable.

Cross-border teams should also identify which timestamp controls internal reporting. Blockchain confirmation, the processor’s payment status, and final settlement may occur at different moments. If those events are recorded inconsistently, a sale can appear in the order system before finance can account for the proceeds. Sample exports from the candidate provider are therefore more informative than a screenshot of its dashboard.

Provider choices by settlement workflow

1: CryptoProcessing and broader payment operations

CryptoProcessing combines acceptance, conversion, fiat settlement, and business wallet functions. A company collecting several digital assets can assess how the platform records exchange rates, delivers settlement documentation, and moves proceeds into the operational balance. Test exceptions alongside successful invoices so the settlement record covers both cases.

2: Triple-A and regulated global payments

Triple-A handles stablecoin collections and payouts, with settlement options in supported local currencies. That range is relevant to companies separating the currency a buyer sends from the currency suppliers receive. Confirm which conversion and reporting arrangements apply to the merchant’s entity.

3: CoinGate and online storefronts

CoinGate connects plugins, payment buttons, and APIs to stablecoin acceptance and fiat settlement. It also offers a payout API and batch disbursements. For international merchants, the relevant question is whether incoming receipts, conversions, and supplier transfers can be reconciled in the same accounting process.

4: NOWPayments and currency coverage

NOWPayments offers a wide choice of cryptocurrencies, along with payment links, invoices, plugins, API tools, and mass payouts. Its broad asset support may be useful in markets where customers hold different coins. Merchants should determine which fiat arrangements are available through the applicable partners.

5: BitPay and mainstream cryptocurrency use

BitPay handles Bitcoin, other major digital assets, stablecoins, invoices, and fiat settlement. BitPay Send adds a separate route for funded crypto disbursements to vendors or affiliates. Document conversion timing and recipient requirements for each product separately; checkout and payout transactions can follow different terms.

6: CoinPayments and token-oriented audiences

CoinPayments provides multi-coin payment processing and wallet-related tools. Crypto-native businesses with diverse token audiences may want to test its acceptance coverage. Settlement methods and payouts warrant a separate check because they depend on the selected configuration.

7: Coinbase Business

Coinbase Commerce’s legacy portal closed after March 31, 2026. Coinbase Business offers stablecoin payment links, invoices, checkout tools, custody, and payouts. Its payment tools accept USDC and, in the U.S. and select jurisdictions, USDT, with receipts settling in USDC by default. Business-account eligibility remains limited to qualifying entities in the U.S. and Singapore.

Match the platform to the merchant model

An ecommerce operation generally needs smooth checkout, reliable status notifications, refunds, and settlement visibility. A SaaS business may care more about invoicing, developer tools, and support for recurring payment workflows. iGaming businesses usually place greater weight on uptime, transaction monitoring, volume handling, and access to funds.

Marketplaces and affiliate networks need to specify how funds move from the platform balance to recipients. Stablecoin and local-currency payouts can serve different obligations. The procurement review should include recipient screening, transfer approval, conversion costs, and the reporting that connects each disbursement to the underlying sale.

Test the complete route before launch

The merchant should run sample payments in the intended currencies, confirm the settlement timeline, review the reports produced, and model a payout or refund. It should also document who holds funds at every stage. Any physical retail component calls for a separate review of a crypto POS terminal and the way in-person transactions appear in finance records.

The useful comparison is the one finance can reproduce: an incoming payment, the conversion rate, the booked settlement, and an outgoing transfer where required. Don’t approve an international rollout until those records agree for each intended settlement currency.

An avid writer with a keen interest in technological developments, he focuses on making complex topics accessible to readers while examining their impact on businesses and everyday users.

item.title: Why Most Apps Don’t Scale (and How to Fix Them)
item.description:
Most of what gets called a scaling problem has nothing to do with traffic. My text scanning app had a stretch of about seven weeks when some scans failed with “couldn’t complete this scan,” and traffic had nothing to do with it. A model upgrade slowed scans, and the slowdown showed up everywhere the system quietly assumed the model would be fast.

This is that story, plus the general mechanics behind it. The production numbers come from my monitoring and commit history. Where I use made-up numbers to show the arithmetic, I say so.

A few terms

Scalability is whether adding resources gets you proportionally more throughput, meaning more completed work per second, without making latency worse. Reliability is whether the system still gives correct answers in reasonable time while part of it is failing.

From the outside, the two look the same. An overloaded system and a hung dependency produce the same timeout, the same error message and the same red line on a dashboard. That’s why “it doesn’t scale” gets said about failures that have nothing to do with load.

A few more terms help:

  • Latency is best read as a distribution. The p50 is the typical request, and the p99 is what one user in a hundred gets.
  • Saturation is work waiting in a queue. It’s different from utilization, which is how busy something is.
  • Vertical scaling means a bigger machine.
  • Horizontal scaling means more machines. It only helps if the bottleneck is the thing you’re adding more of.

Two formulas are worth knowing. Little’s Law says the number of requests in flight equals arrival rate times latency. And for a single server with random arrivals, mean response time is service time divided by one minus utilization. That’s twice the service time at 50% busy, five times at 80% and ten times at 90%. This curve is why a system that looks fine at 70% can fall over at 90%.

How the app works

You photograph a page. The phone resizes and encodes it, and a Firebase function sends it to a model and returns the text while you watch a spinner.

The first version used Google Cloud Vision for OCR, plus a separate OpenAI call for titles and corrections. The current one uses an LLM-based pipeline. Pages go in, and JSON comes out with the language, the raw text, a corrected version, a title, and optionally a summary and some additional insights. That’s one dependency instead of two, and far less code. On gemini-2.0-flash-lite, the daily p50 was 6.6–7.4 seconds and the p95 was 14–17 seconds, comfortably inside the function’s 60-second deadline.

A slower model

Then I moved to gemini-2.5-flash-lite, and the numbers shifted:

The median got a little slower, but the tail is where it hurt. For seven weeks, p99 sat at the 60-second timeout every day, and in one two-week window at least 200 scans ended in a 504 at 59.99 seconds.

Retries amplified it. The retry logic suited a fast model: try a failed call twice more, and regenerate if the JSON came back malformed. That’s up to six model calls for one scan. At seven seconds a call that’s harmless. During a slow patch, though, the first attempt could take most of the minute, and each retry started with less time than the attempt before it had needed.

Two fixes

The first fix gave each request a time budget instead of a pile of independent attempts. The function’s deadline went from 60 to 300 seconds, about five times the slowest successful scan. Every model call now receives the same absolute deadline, each attempt has its own cap, and a retry only starts if at least 12 seconds are left.

The second went after the bottleneck. I ran a control benchmark, the same model on a different endpoint, and it was just as slow. That ruled out the region and pointed at the model. Moving to gemini-3.1-flash-lite roughly halved scan times. A tax document went from 13.6–15.5 seconds to 7.3–12.9, with no failures across 30 calls.

What’s different when the bottleneck is a model

The interesting lessons weren’t about timeouts. They were about what changes when the slowest thing in your system is a model you rent.

The response schema is a latency budget. Sending lower-resolution images cut input tokens by 25% and didn’t change latency at all, because generation time depends on how much the model writes, not how much it reads. Every field in the JSON is text the model produces while someone watches a spinner. The app already asks for a smaller schema when the user hasn’t requested a summary or insights, and I now treat each new field as a latency decision.

A model version is a capacity change with an expiry date. Switching versions moved p95 by several seconds without any other code changing. And you don’t fully control the timing. Hosted models get retired, and the version I’d just moved away from was scheduled for retirement less than three months later anyway. Each forced migration is effectively a load test, so it’s worth keeping a benchmark you can rerun on the next candidate.

Concurrency sets the blast radius. By default, each instance of the function serves up to 80 requests at once. One small guard in the fix handles the late failure of a model call that has already lost the race against its timer. Without it, Node 22 would treat that failure as fatal, and the process would take every in-flight scan down with it. High concurrency saves money and cold starts. It also makes the instance, rather than the request, the unit of failure.

Success-only metrics flatter you. During the slow period, the last 1,000 successful requests had a p99 of 26.9 seconds, which looks healthy. Across all requests, p99 was 60. Measuring only successes hides exactly the slow requests you care about. And when p99 equals your timeout, you’re really measuring the timeout.

Deadlines have to nest

Raising a server deadline has a side effect worth knowing about. The Android SDK’s default timeout for these calls is 70 seconds, and Flutter’s is 60. So with a 290-second server budget, a long scan can fail on the phone while the server keeps working, paying for a result nobody will see. Tap scan again and two generations run for one page. The failure also stops showing up as a server error, so it appears only in client crash reports.

The fix is to line the numbers up: the client timeout longer than the server deadline, and the server deadline longer than the total of the attempt caps. You can set the client timeout explicitly. Or you can send the client’s deadline with the request and budget everything from that, which Google’s SRE book calls deadline propagation.

The textbook part, briefly

Queueing. Little’s Law turns slowness into concurrency. With made-up numbers: at 10 scans a second and 8 seconds each, 80 scans are in flight, enough to fill one instance. If the model slows to 30 seconds, the same traffic means 300 in flight across four instances, nearly all of them waiting. Autoscaling absorbs the wait and bills you for it.

Contention. Requests that need the same row or lock take turns. If a global UPDATE stats SET scans = scans + 1 holds its lock for 5 ms, that caps you at 200 scans a second, however many servers you add (made-up numbers again). Sharded counters avoid the queue, and so does appending events and summing them later.

Retry amplification. Retries multiply across layers. Google’s SRE book describes three layers making four attempts each, which turns one user action into 64 attempts at the bottom, all arriving exactly when the dependency is struggling. To keep that in check:

  • retry at one layer only
  • cap retries by the time remaining
  • add jitter
  • keep retries under a budget (the book’s example is 10% of requests)

Connection limits catch people out on serverless. Postgres defaults to 100 connections, three of them reserved for superusers, and every instance opens its own pool. My app doesn’t use Postgres, but suppose it did, with 20 connections per instance. The slow-model scenario above pushes you to six instances and 120 connections, and every connection past the 97th fails. A pooler like PgBouncer, smaller pools and an instance cap based on the connection limit all prevent it.

When the “unscalable” choice is right

One function. I’d keep the scan path as a single function. An in-process call takes nanoseconds. A call to another service adds latency and new ways to fail, such as timeouts, dropped connections and the other service being down. Splitting the scan into services would add all of that to a request whose cost is already one model call.

Synchronous calls are fine too, as long as scans usually finish well inside the client timeout. Going async means a job store, idempotency keys and a way to push results back. It also adds new failure modes, such as a finished job whose notification never arrives. It starts to make sense for work that can outlast the client timeout, like a long multi-page scan. A queue doesn’t remove a bottleneck. It moves the waiting somewhere you control.

Relational databases stay the right choice for a long time if you need transactions, constraints or joins. Sharding gives up cross-shard joins and transactions, and before you get there you have plenty of room:

  • query plans
  • connection pooling
  • read replicas
  • partitioning by time
  • a bigger instance.

What I’d do next time

  • Measure all requests. Include failures in latency, and keep percentiles per endpoint and timing per dependency.
  • Line latency graphs up against deploy history. That’s how this slowdown was traced to a single deploy.
  • Find the bottleneck and change one thing at a time against a control. Then check that the number of users feel actually moved.
  • Load-test at a fixed arrival rate, for example with k6’s constant-arrival-rate. Looping virtual users slow down when your server does, which hides the problem; the effect is called coordinated omission. Then stub the model with long delays and 429s, and watch what the timeouts, retries and client do.
  • Benchmark every model change as if it were a capacity change.

Most of this incident wasn’t exotic. It was a set of settings sized for a fast model meeting a slower one. The useful habit is to write those numbers down, check that they nest, and test them against the real latency distribution, failures included.

Amer Sheeny

  • keep retries under a budget (the book’s example is 10% of requests)

Connection limits catch people out on serverless. Postgres defaults to 100 connections, three of them reserved for superusers, and every instance opens its own pool. My app doesn’t use Postgres, but suppose it did, with 20 connections per instance. The slow-model scenario above pushes you to six instances and 120 connections, and every connection past the 97th fails. A pooler like PgBouncer, smaller pools and an instance cap based on the connection limit all prevent it.

When the “unscalable” choice is right

One function. I’d keep the scan path as a single function. An in-process call takes nanoseconds. A call to another service adds latency and new ways to fail, such as timeouts, dropped connections and the other service being down. Splitting the scan into services would add all of that to a request whose cost is already one model call.

Synchronous calls are fine too, as long as scans usually finish well inside the client timeout. Going async means a job store, idempotency keys and a way to push results back. It also adds new failure modes, such as a finished job whose notification never arrives. It starts to make sense for work that can outlast the client timeout, like a long multi-page scan. A queue doesn’t remove a bottleneck. It moves the waiting somewhere you control.

Relational databases stay the right choice for a long time if you need transactions, constraints or joins. Sharding gives up cross-shard joins and transactions, and before you get there you have plenty of room:

  • query plans
  • connection pooling
  • read replicas
  • partitioning by time
  • a bigger instance.

What I’d do next time

  • Measure all requests. Include failures in latency, and keep percentiles per endpoint and timing per dependency.

  • Find the bottleneck and change one thing at a time against a control. Then check that the number of users feel actually moved.
  • Load-test at a fixed arrival rate, for example with k6’s constant-arrival-rate. Looping virtual users slow down when your server does, which hides the problem; the effect is called coordinated omission. Then stub the model with long delays and 429s, and watch what the timeouts, retries and client do.
  • Benchmark every model change as if it were a capacity change.

Most of this incident wasn’t exotic. It was a set of settings sized for a fast model meeting a slower one. The useful habit is to write those numbers down, check that they nest, and test them against the real latency distribution, failures included.

item.title: JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard confirm vendor incidents after n0n leak claims
item.description:
JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard acknowledged cyber incidents involving third-party service providers on Thursday, November 19, after the extortion group n0n posted files it claimed contained records linked to the three companies.

JPMorgan said it believes attackers accessed marketing data held by its vendors, which may include customer names and email addresses. Mastercard confirmed that a provider incident exposed email addresses belonging to a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a benefits program. It said the incident did not affect its payment network or card use.

Visa told Reuters that it linked the claims to an incident involving a service provider in the Asia-Pacific region. Visa said its own systems and payment data were unaffected. It did not confirm that customer records were exposed.

What the files contained

Reuters reported that n0n posted claims and files relating to Visa and Mastercard on November 16. Hackread.com reviewed the files posted by the group and counted 16,541 unique email addresses in the material attributed to JPMorgan Chase, 7,815 in the files attributed to Visa and 3,210 in those attributed to Mastercard. These figures count distinct email addresses within each dataset. They do not establish how many customers were affected.

Hackread.com’s review also found entries for Hong Kong, Taiwan, South Korea, Japan, the Philippines, Singapore, Malaysia, Australia and Macau in the files attributed to Visa. The files attributed to Mastercard included marketing records for markets in North America, the Middle East and Africa.

None of the three companies named the providers involved, and it remains unclear whether the incidents involved a common vendor. Mastercard said it had contained the exposure and was working with the provider to assist affected cardholders. JPMorgan said it would contact affected customers where appropriate and offer free credit monitoring.

The n0n group has been active since September 2026. The Wall Street Journal, citing cybersecurity firm Recorded Future, reported that the group steals corporate data for extortion and recruits other hackers to gain access to company networks.

Chase says its banking outage was unrelated

JPMorgan said the vendor incident was unrelated to the November 16 Chase outage, which it attributed to a software bug affecting its internal hardware systems.

Email addresses, phone numbers and details about a customer’s relationship with a bank or card provider can make fake fraud alerts or benefits messages more convincing. If a message asks you to verify your account or claim a benefit, open your bank’s app directly or call the number on the back of your card. A message that mentions a program you actually use can still be a scam.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: 4 Best XRP Lending Platforms Compared by Security, LTV, and Speed
item.description:
Borrowing against XRP allows cryptocurrency holders to access funds without selling their assets. However, loan-to-value (LTV) limits, interest rates, collateral storage arrangements, and repayment conditions vary considerably between lenders.

Some platforms offer higher borrowing limits and faster access to funds, while others focus on third-party custody, established credit accounts, or decentralised lending protocols. Comparing these differences matters, especially because XRP price movements can affect collateral requirements and trigger liquidation.

The 4 Best XRP Lending Platforms: Quick List

  • CoinRabbit: crypto loans with up to 90% starting LTV, issued within 10 minutes, with minimums from $25 depending on the asset.
  • Arch: Up to 45% starting LTV, third-party custody through Anchorage Digital, and a $25,000 minimum loan.
  • Nexo: XRP-backed credit lines with up to 30% LTV and interest rates determined by region and loyalty tier.
  • Coinbase: Onchain XRP-backed loans through Morpho, with borrowing of up to $100,000 in USDC.

Understanding XRP-Backed Loans

XRP-backed lending allows holders to use their cryptocurrency as collateral to obtain cash or stablecoins. Instead of selling XRP, borrowers deposit it with a lending service or into a supported lending protocol and receive funds based on the collateral’s market value.

The amount available depends largely on the loan-to-value ratio. For example, a 50% LTV allows a borrower to receive $5,000 against $10,000 worth of XRP. Higher LTV ratios provide access to more funds but leave less room for price declines before borrowers must add collateral or repay.

XRP holders also face fewer lending options compared with Bitcoin and Ethereum holders, making it important to examine each provider’s terms rather than relying on advertised interest rates alone.

Research Scope and Method

This comparison examines four platforms offering XRP-backed borrowing, using five criteria: collateral security, starting LTV, funding speed, minimum loan requirements, and interest rate structure.

The figures are based on publicly stated platform terms as of November 2026. They should be treated as advertised conditions rather than independently verified performance guarantees. Rates, asset eligibility, and borrowing limits can also vary by jurisdiction and account status. To illustrate how borrowing limits differ, the comparison uses a hypothetical holder with $100,000 worth of XRP.

Key Findings

  • Borrowing limits differ substantially. Advertised maximum starting LTVs range from 30% to 90%, giving borrowers very different levels of access to funds.
  • Minimum loan amounts vary. Some services accommodate relatively small loans, while others require collateral sufficient to support borrowing of at least $25,000.
  • Interest calculations are not uniform. Fixed-rate loans, daily compounding interest, and variable onchain borrowing rates make direct comparisons more complicated.
  • Custody arrangements differ. Borrowers may encounter segregated cold storage, independent custodians, centralised platform accounts, or blockchain-based smart contracts.
  • Liquidation remains a significant consideration. A high starting LTV reduces the amount XRP can decline before the loan becomes subject to additional collateral requirements or liquidation.

XRP Lending Platforms Compared

The following table summarises the published terms of the four services, presented in the same order as the Quick List.

The maximum LTV figures do not represent equivalent risk levels. Borrowers must also consider liquidation thresholds, margin call procedures, fees, and whether additional collateral can be deposited during market declines.

Platform Profiles

CoinRabbit

Operating since 2020, the platform offers XRP-backed loans with selectable starting LTV ratios of 50%, 65%, 80%, and 90%. According to its published terms, collateral is held in segregated cold multisig wallets, with a stated policy of maintaining full reserves and not rehypothecating deposited assets.

Borrowers can receive stablecoins, including USDT and USDC, without undergoing a traditional credit check. The service advertises loan issuance within 10 minutes.

Interest rates start at 11.95% APR and remain fixed for the agreed loan period. Both fixed-term and open-ended borrowing arrangements are available. Additional features include automatic collateral top-ups from a linked wallet and a loan restoration mechanism for eligible liquidated positions.

With a maximum advertised starting LTV of 90%, a holder pledging $100,000 in XRP could borrow up to $90,000, subject to the platform’s terms. However, borrowing at such a high percentage leaves relatively little protection against a decline in XRP’s price. Borrowers should examine the liquidation threshold and collateral requirements before selecting the maximum available amount.

Arch

Arch focuses on larger cryptocurrency-backed loans and uses Anchorage Digital for collateral custody. The company states that pledged assets are held separately and are not rehypothecated.

XRP-backed loans begin at $25,000, with a maximum starting LTV of 45%. The platform specifies a margin call threshold of 55% LTV and a 24-hour period to address collateral shortfalls. Partial liquidation can occur at 65% LTV.

Pricing depends on the loan amount. Published rates range from 13.50% APR for loans between $25,000 and $500,000, including a 1.50% origination fee, to 8.50% APR for loans exceeding $5 million. Loan terms extend to 12 months, with identity verification and approval required before funding. Borrowers can receive funds through USD wire transfers or USDC.

For the $100,000 XRP example, the maximum initial loan would be $45,000. The relatively low starting LTV provides more room for collateral price declines than higher-LTV products, although borrowers must still monitor the stated margin call and liquidation levels.

Nexo

Nexo provides cryptocurrency-backed credit lines, allowing eligible customers to borrow against supported digital assets, including XRP. The platform lists a maximum XRP LTV of 30%, placing its borrowing limit below those of the first two lenders in this comparison.

Advertised interest rates begin at 1.9%, but eligibility depends on factors such as the borrower’s region and loyalty tier. Interest accrues daily and compounds, making the effective borrowing cost dependent on the applicable rate and repayment period. Borrowers can repay according to their own schedule, subject to the credit line’s conditions.

Stablecoin withdrawals begin at $50, while bank transfers require a minimum of $500. The platform lists daily withdrawal limits of up to $2 million, with funds arriving on the same business day or within five business days, depending on the payment method. A borrower providing $100,000 worth of XRP could access up to $30,000 at the published maximum LTV.

The service is particularly relevant to existing account holders seeking a credit line rather than a separate fixed-term loan. However, customers should review their applicable borrowing rate, interest calculation, and collateral requirements before proceeding.

Coinbase

Coinbase supports XRP-backed borrowing through its integration with Morpho, a decentralised lending protocol. Unlike traditional lending arrangements, the collateral is managed through blockchain-based smart contracts, while borrowers receive USDC through the Coinbase application.

The platform lists a maximum XRP-backed borrowing amount of $100,000, with liquidation occurring when the position reaches 86% LTV. This 86% figure represents the liquidation threshold, not the maximum initial borrowing ratio. The actual amount available to a borrower depends on the lending market’s permitted starting LTV and other applicable restrictions.

Interest rates are variable and determined by conditions in the Morpho lending market. Borrowers can repay according to their preferred schedule, provided the position remains within the protocol’s collateral requirements.

The onchain arrangement offers a different custody model, but introduces smart contract, protocol, and variable-rate risks alongside XRP price volatility. Borrowers should review both the initial borrowing limit and the liquidation threshold before opening a position.

Which Crypto Lending Platforms Accept XRP?

Several centralised and decentralised lending services support XRP as collateral, although their borrowing arrangements differ. Centralised lenders generally manage collateral custody, credit approvals, and liquidation procedures through their own systems or external custodians. Decentralised lending protocols instead rely on smart contracts to hold collateral and enforce borrowing requirements.

Neither arrangement eliminates risk. Custodial lenders require borrowers to assess operational security, asset segregation, and counterparty exposure. Onchain loans introduce technical risks associated with smart contracts, blockchain infrastructure, and lending market conditions. The appropriate choice depends on the borrower’s desired loan size, tolerance for liquidation risk, and preference for custodial or onchain arrangements.

How to Borrow Against XRP

The general process for borrowing against XRP is similar across most lending services, although the details differ between providers.

  • Compare borrowing terms. Examine the maximum starting LTV, interest rate, repayment requirements, fees, and liquidation conditions.
  • Choose a loan amount. Select an amount that leaves sufficient collateral value to withstand XRP price fluctuations.
  • Complete the required verification. Some lenders require identity checks, while others use wallet-based lending arrangements.
  • Deposit XRP as collateral. Transfer assets to the lender’s designated address or approved smart contract.
  • Receive the loan. Depending on the service, funds may be issued in stablecoins or transferred through a supported banking method.
  • Repay the outstanding balance. Repayment of principal, interest, and applicable charges allows borrowers to recover their remaining collateral, subject to the platform’s conditions.

Before depositing cryptocurrency, borrowers should verify the receiving address, supported blockchain network, and withdrawal conditions. A transfer to an incorrect address or unsupported network can result in permanent loss of funds.

Why XRP Price Volatility Matters

The principal risk in XRP-backed borrowing is that the collateral’s value can decline while the outstanding debt remains unchanged. Consider a borrower who deposits $100,000 in XRP and receives a $70,000 loan. The starting LTV is 70%.

If the XRP collateral loses 20% of its value, its market value falls to $80,000. Assuming the outstanding loan remains $70,000, the LTV increases to 87.5%. That increase can trigger liquidation if the lender’s threshold has been exceeded, even though the borrower has not withdrawn additional funds.

Borrowers can reduce this risk by selecting a lower initial LTV, adding more collateral when permitted, or repaying part of the outstanding loan. Interest charges can also increase the effective LTV over time, particularly when interest compounds.

What the Comparison Means for XRP Holders

The four lending services address different borrowing requirements. For smaller loans, minimum borrowing amounts and funding times are important considerations. Someone seeking a relatively modest stablecoin loan may find a $25,000 minimum impractical, regardless of the interest rate.

Larger borrowers may place greater importance on custody arrangements, published interest schedules, and the treatment of collateral during market declines. Existing credit platform customers may prefer borrowing through an account they already use, while borrowers familiar with decentralised finance may choose smart contract-based lending.

However, the highest available LTV is not automatically the most favourable option. It allows more borrowing against the same collateral, but also reduces the protection available when XRP declines in value.

Interest rates require similar attention. An advertised starting rate may depend on eligibility conditions, account tiers, loan size, or other factors that affect the final cost. For borrowers comparing these services, the most useful approach is to calculate the total repayment cost, determine how much XRP can fall before liquidation, and understand who controls the pledged assets.

Conclusion

XRP-backed lending provides an alternative to selling cryptocurrency when holders need access to funds. However, the available products differ in borrowing limits, collateral custody, interest calculations, and liquidation procedures.

The comparison shows that higher LTV limits offer greater access to funds but also increase exposure to XRP price volatility. Lower-LTV products restrict borrowing capacity while providing more room for collateral values to decline.

Borrowers should therefore assess the full loan conditions rather than selecting a lender based on advertised rates or funding speed alone. The deciding factors are the amount borrowed, total cost, collateral security, and the consequences of a decline in XRP’s market value.

Disclaimer: This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute financial or investment advice. Cryptocurrency-backed loans carry significant risks, including price volatility, margin calls, liquidation, and possible loss of collateral. Interest rates, lending terms, and platform availability may change. Readers should conduct their own research, review the lender’s terms and conditions, and consult a qualified financial adviser before making borrowing or investment decisions.

item.title: Fake GTA VI Streaming Client Installs Data-Stealing Malware on Windows PCs
item.description:
Grand Theft Auto VI’s scams have not gone away with the game’s release. Hackread.com has previously reported fake beta downloads, early-access offers and leaked-game scams. Now, scammers are using the lack of an official PC version to deliver a fake streaming client that infects Windows computers with malware.

Bitdefender discovered this new scam after identifying a website (gta6cloud.nexus) claiming its GTA VI cloud client lets PC users stream the game from an Xbox or PlayStation. The catch here is that this site offers a ZIP download but also gives visitors another way to install it- asking them to press Win+R, paste a PowerShell command and run it.

How the attack works

This is a ClickFix attack, where victims are tricked into running commands on their own computers. The command bypasses PowerShell’s execution policy, downloads a script from the site and runs it, eventually fetching and launching GTA6Cloud.exe.

The fake client plays the GTA VI trailer and displays a game-themed page while downloading two more files, loadperf.dll and unlodctr.exe, from velmontriq.net. The files are placed in a hidden folder on the computer.

A fake client hides a much bigger infection

The attackers use DLL sideloading to run their malicious code through unlodctr.exe, which is a legitimate Windows utility. A malicious DLL (loadperf.dll) is placed with it that gets loaded when the program runs. This gives the attackers a way to execute their code through a trusted executable.

Additionally, it contains another payload: PhotoCache.exe. This file is injected into legitimate Windows processes instead of being saved as a separate executable.

The injected payload is a Rust-based information stealer. In its research shared with Hackread.com, Bitdefender explained that it uses legitimate Windows tools and processes to stay hidden while collecting data from infected computers.

This includes browser passwords, cookies and tokens, Discord and Steam data, crypto wallets, AI service credentials and developer API keys. It can also access clipboard data and take screenshots. item.title: Hackers Using Email Bombing Before Posing as IT Support on Microsoft Teams
item.description:
Fortra warns of an email bombing campaign where hackers flood work inboxes, then pose as IT support on Microsoft Teams to get access to work accounts.

Receiving thousands of unwanted emails can be more than an inbox problem because cybercriminals are using this strategy to approach employees on Microsoft Teams, pretending to be IT support staff and offering help to stop the messages.

Fortra Intelligence and Research Experts (FIRE) have discovered and reported impersonation fraud cases where attackers first bombard employees with subscription emails and then contact them through Teams. The callers claim to be from the company’s IT department and provide instructions to stop the messages. But these instructions are intended to compromise the employee’s account or computer.

The emails are generated through a technique called subscription bombing, in which hackers enter a target’s email address into newsletter sign-up pages, registration forms and other websites; the services then send confirmation emails and other notifications to the address.

According to FIRE’s observations, shared with Hackread.com, these campaigns generate around 1,000 emails a day and up to 10,000 messages are sent during an active campaign. There’s evidence suggesting that attackers may be using AI agents to find websites with sign-up forms and submit email addresses automatically. Mailchimp and its email delivery service Mandrill were the most commonly observed platforms, followed by Amazon SES and SendGrid.

Posing as internal IT staff, these fake callers give victims verbal and email instructions to stop the incoming messages, but Fortra says they are “attempting to compromise the user account, system, or both.”

Gaining access to an employee’s account could expose company emails, files and other resources the account can reach, while access to the computer could also expose other systems. The actual impact would depend on what access the attackers manage to obtain.

Forta researchers also found phishing emails during some of these attacks involving messages that used fake loading screens and verification steps to make their pages look genuine, but they could not conclude whether those behind these emails were the same attackers making the Teams calls.

Explaining the reason behind the approach, FIRE wrote that attackers are “creating the incident and then attempting to own the response.” That’s an important distinction- the employee is not simply dealing with unwanted mail but may also be approached by the person responsible for it.

This is not the first report of Teams being abused by cybercriminals to pose as IT staff. In October, Hackread reported the Arctic Wolf Labs research revealing over 400 incidents involving fake IT support accounts contacting employees through external Teams chats.

Fortra advises employees to avoid attending unexpected support calls and personally contact their IT department through official channels because simply knowing about the email flood doesn’t prove they are genuine IT support staff.

Researchers also suggest that security teams should review external access in Teams, preserve suspicious emails, and immediately check account activity if an employee followed the caller’s instructions.
